## 1 - Load data

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, output=FALSE}
# getwd() output is /Users/rosehedderman/Desktop/CDN/BCRP_Beginner_1hr/
base_dir <- "/Users/rosehedderman/Desktop/CDN/BCRP_Beginner_1hr/data"
sample_dirs <- list.dirs(base_dir, recursive = FALSE)
valid_dirs <- sample_dirs[
  file.exists(file.path(sample_dirs, "sample_filtered_feature_bc_matrix"))
]

# Read 10X data
data_list <- lapply(valid_dirs, function(dir) {
  Read10X(data.dir = file.path(dir, "sample_filtered_feature_bc_matrix"))
})
names(data_list) <- basename(sample_dirs)

# Create Seurat Objects
seurat_list <- lapply(names(data_list), function(name) {
  CreateSeuratObject(counts = data_list[[name]], project = name)
})
names(seurat_list) <- names(data_list)

# Merge objects into one
se <- merge(
  x = seurat_list[[1]],
  y = seurat_list[-1],
  add.cell.ids = names(seurat_list)
)
se
```

Join counts layers into one using Seurat's JoinLayers.

```{r}
se <- JoinLayers(se)
Layers(se)
```

Let's peek at the metadata after loading.

```{r}
# dim(se@meta.data)
head(se@meta.data)
```

### Load Known Metadata

To add more metadata, we can join other dataframes to se\@meta.data.
Here, Donor 1 has automated cell type annotations that we can use as a
reference.

```{r}
donor1_ct <- read_csv(paste0(base_dir, "/HealthyDonor1/cell_types/cell_types.csv"))
# head(donor1_ct)
```

Fix barcodes in cell_types dataframe to merge to Seurat object metadata.

```{r}
donor1_ct <- donor1_ct %>%
  mutate(barcode = paste0("HealthyDonor1_", barcode))
donor1_ct %>% tail(3)
```

### Join Metadata

```{r}
se@meta.data <- se@meta.data %>%
  rownames_to_column("barcode") %>%
  rename(Donor = orig.ident) %>%
  left_join(donor1_ct, by = "barcode") %>%
  column_to_rownames("barcode")
# head(se@meta.data)
```

The table view is helpful for smaller scale, complete comparisons.

```{r}
table(se@meta.data$coarse_cell_type, se@meta.data$Donor)
```

### Data exploration

Mini Glossary:

-   **Unique molecular identifier (UMI)**: unique molecular barcode
    added to each transcript before PCR amplification to correct for
    biases during that process.\
-   **Library size**: total number of UMIs detected for each cell.\
-   **Library complexity**: number of genes that have expression \> 0 in
    each cell. The more genes detected in a cell the more complex a cell
    is. Examples of low complexity cells are platelets and red blood
    cells which can be confounded with low quality cells if not assessed
    properly.

The aim is to visualize the available data to catch potential library prep issues and batch effects.

#### Library Size

nCount_RNA is the number of UMIs per cell. This is a measure of the
total number of transcripts detected in a cell and is the way to
visualize library size.

```{r, fig.width=4, fig.height=3}
# Visualize the UMI counts across samples.
ggplot(se@meta.data, aes(x = nCount_RNA, fill = Donor)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.7) + # color = "#6abcb6", fill = "#6abcb6", 
    scale_x_continuous(
        transform = "log10",
        labels = scales::unit_format(unit = "K", scale = 1e-3)) +
    theme_classic()
```

#### Library Complexity

nFeature_RNA is the number of genes detected in a cell. Cells with few genes and few UMIs are considered low quality.

```{r, fig.width=4, fig.height=3}
# Visualize the feature (gene) counts across samples.
ggplot(se@meta.data, aes(x = nFeature_RNA, fill = Donor)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.7) + # color = "#6abcb6", fill = "#6abcb6", 
    scale_x_continuous(
        labels = scales::unit_format(unit = "K", scale = 1e-3)) +
    theme_classic()
```

## 2 - Quality Control

QC is the process of filtering out “bad” data. This makes it a subjective process, making well-informed decisions is key to avoid removing biological signal. In this context, being conservative in what we call “poor quality” cells is best practice.

The main pitfall in this step is to be too stringent. This may lead to removing true biological signal. Some examples of cells that might be filtered out during the QC process are neutrophils, platelets, and erythrocytes since they have low library size and complexity.

Doublets can be confounded with transitioning cells or cells with mixed phenotypes. Therefore, it is very important that we are very careful when calling a cell a doublet! Otherwise, we might be removing very interesting biology.

Add percentage of common features

```{r}
# Calculate the percentage of mitochondrial genes
se <- PercentageFeatureSet(se, pattern = "^MT-", col.name = "perc.mt")
# Calculate the percentage of ribosomal genes
se <- PercentageFeatureSet(se, pattern = "^RPS|^RPL", col.name = "perc.ribo")
# Calculate the percentage of hemoglobin genes
se <- PercentageFeatureSet(se, pattern = "^HB[^(P)]", col.name = "perc.hb")
```

Visualize by sample

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
# Plot features by Sample together
VlnPlot(se,
  group.by = "Donor",
  features = c("perc.mt", "perc.ribo", "perc.hb"),
  # log = TRUE,
  pt.size = 0
  ) &
    NoLegend()
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=3}
# Comparison of mitochondrial and hemoglobin genes
p1 <- se@meta.data %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x = perc.mt, y = perc.hb, color = Donor)) +
    geom_point() +
    # scale_color_manual(values = pal) +
    theme_classic()
p2 <- se@meta.data %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x = perc.mt, y = perc.hb, color = `coarse_cell_type`)) +
    geom_point() +
    # scale_color_manual(values = donor_pal) +
    theme_classic() 
p1 | p2
```

### Doublets!

Doublet detection and removal is sensitive because you don’t want to remove any valuable outliers but still take into consideration the noisiness of the data.

`DoubletFinder` uses a nearest neighbor approach to identify doublets. The package has a function called `doubletFinder` that takes in a Seurat object and returns a Seurat object with doublet information added in the metadata.

**How it Works**

1.  DoubletFinder combines random cell's gene expression profiles to create "fake doublets."
2.  Artificial doublets are inserted into the data
3.  Dimensionality reduction and a KNN graph is built with our cells and the fake doublets.
4.  On the k-nearest neighbor graph each cell has k most-similar neighbors. pANN is the proportion of each cell's neighbors that are "fake doublets".
5.  A high pANN value indicates that a larger proportion of the cells around a specific cell in the kNN graph are "fake doublets" suggesting that the cell has a transcriptome similar to a doublet.

Cells in transitioning states or cells with mixed phenotpyes can be mistaken for doublets. It is important not to disregard cells just because they have a large doublet score (pANN value), there might be interesting biological information in these cells!

`DoubletFinder` allows you to set a threshold and will give each cell a categorical result of 'Singlet' or 'Doublet'. We suggest looking at the raw pANN values to understand the distribution of these cells and make threshold adjustments accordingly.

More information can be found in the CDN's QC notebook or other public resources.

### Label cell quality

For the sake of preserving valuable data, we label low quality cells early on and filter them out later in the analysis. 

```{r}
se@meta.data <- se@meta.data %>%
  mutate(
    quality = if_else(
        nFeature_RNA > 200 & nCount_RNA > 500 & perc.mt < 15, "good quality", "bad quality"),
    quality = factor(quality, levels = c("bad quality", "good quality"))
    )
```

# 3 - Preprocessing

1.  Normalization
2.  Highly Variable Gene Selection
3.  Dimensionality Reduction

### A - Normalization

TOFIX: According to the documentation, this function does the
following - Feature counts for each cell are divided by the total counts
for that cell and multiplied by the scale.factor. This is then
natural-log transformed using log1p.

```{r}
se@assays$RNA$counts[15:25, 15:30]
```

```{r}
se <- NormalizeData(se, normalization.method = "LogNormalize", scale.factor = 1e4)

se@assays$RNA$data[15:25, 15:30]
```

### B - Highly Variable Gene Selection

TOFIX: Subsetting our count matrix to highly variable genes is a key
step for downstream analysis. We need to reduce the dimensions of the
count matrix so that we can carry out downstream tasks such as PCA.

The intutition behind selecting HVG is that those genes with highest
variability capture high level biological variability in our datasets
and can help us identify the populations present in our dataset.

To do this we can use the vst method: - First, fits a line to the
relationship of log(variance) and log(mean) using local polynomial
regression (loess). - Then standardizes the feature values using the
observed mean and expected variance (given by the fitted line). -
Feature variance is then calculated on the standardized values after
clipping to a maximum (see clip.max parameter).

```{r}
se <- FindVariableFeatures(se, nfeatures = 3000, selection.method = "vst")

# Identify the 50 most highly variable genes
top <- head(VariableFeatures(se), 100)

# plot variable features with and without labels
plot1 <- VariableFeaturePlot(se)
plot2 <- LabelPoints(plot = plot1, points = top, repel = TRUE)
plot2 +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", error = FALSE) +
    scale_y_log10()
```

Once we have those annotated, we will proceed to subsetting our data to
a cell type of interest and RECOMPUTING HVG so that they are updated and
represent the biological variability in this new dataset!

### C - Dimensionality Reduction

Mini Glossary:

-   **Dimensionality Reduction**: The computational process of reducing
    a large data matrix to fewer features.
-   **Latent Space/Embeddings**: A latent space is a hidden set of
    dimensions in the data that could be useful in ways the raw data is
    not.
-   **Feature**: A variable in a sample x variable matrix. In a cell x
    gene matrix, the gene is the feature. In PCA, the principal
    components are the features.
-   **Loadings**: This is the term used to describe the feature
    translation matrix. Which genes are in which PC? The Loadings matrix
    shows the weights of each gene in each PC.

```{r}
se <- se  %>%
    ScaleData(verbose = FALSE, features = VariableFeatures(.)) %>% 
    RunPCA(
        npcs = 30,
        ndims.print = 1:5,
        nfeatures.print = 10
    )

# This is where latent spaces, aka dimensional reductions are stored. If we call it directly, we can see some information about the PCA.
se@reductions$pca
```

#### Using PCA to understand variance in your data

# 4 - INTEGRATION

```{r}
se <- se %>%
  RunUMAP(
    dims = 1:20,
    reduction = "pca",
    reduction.name = "pca_umap",
    verbose = FALSE
  ) %>%
    RunHarmony(
      group.by.vars = 'Donor',
      reduction.uptest = 'pca',
    ) %>%
  RunUMAP(
    dims = 1:20,
    reduction = "harmony",
    reduction.name = "harmony_umap",
    verbose = FALSE
  )
```

```{r, fig.height=4, fig.width=10}
DimPlot(se, 
        reduction = "pca_umap", 
        group.by = "Donor") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  DimPlot(se, 
        reduction = "harmony_umap", 
        group.by = "Donor") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r, fig.height=6, fig.width=8}
DimPlot(se, 
        reduction = "pca_umap", 
        group.by = "fine_cell_type", 
        label = TRUE) + NoLegend()
```

Compare clustering of good and bad quality cells.

P-Value Interpretation in
OSCA(https://bioconductor.org/books/3.17/OSCA.advanced/marker-detection-redux.html#p-value-invalidity)

```{r}
plot_batch_effect_heatmap <- function(
                                     seurat_object, 
                                     latent_space = 'pca', 
                                     num_pcs = 20, 
                                     metadata_columns_to_include = NULL,
                                     plot_title = "Correlation Heatmap of Metadata and PCA Components") {
    metadata <- seurat_object@meta.data
    metadata <- metadata[, metadata_columns_to_include, drop = FALSE]
    pca_data <- Embeddings(seurat_object, latent_space)[, 1:num_pcs] # pull the PCs we want to check

    categorical_cols <- sapply(metadata, function(col) is.factor(col) || is.character(col))
    
    # convert character columns to factors for one-hot encoding
    metadata[categorical_cols] <- lapply(metadata[categorical_cols], as.factor)

    #1hot without removing redundant dummies
    metadata_encoded <- fastDummies::dummy_cols(
        metadata,
        remove_first_dummy = FALSE,
        remove_selected_columns = TRUE)

    combined_data <- cbind(metadata_encoded, pca_data) # combine metadata and PCA data
    
    # calculate the correlation matrix
    correlation_matrix <- cor(combined_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

    # Subset the correlation matrix to include only metadata and PCA components
    metadata_columns <- colnames(metadata_encoded)
    pca_columns <- colnames(pca_data)
    subset_correlation_matrix <- correlation_matrix[metadata_columns, pca_columns, drop = FALSE]
    
    # Check for any NA values in the subset correlation matrix and replace them with 0
    subset_correlation_matrix[is.na(subset_correlation_matrix)] <- 0
    
    # Create the heatmap using corrplot
    corrplot(subset_correlation_matrix, method = "circle", tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
             number.cex = 0.7, tl.cex = 0.7,
             main = plot_title)
}

plot_batch_effect_heatmap(
    se, 
    metadata_columns_to_include = c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA","Donor", "quality"))
```

# Save Whole Object

```{r}
save_dir <- paste0(base_dir, "/annot_lvl1.rds")
```

### Split Object into Sub Types

```{r}
lymphocyte <- subset(se, subset = annotation_lvl1 %in% c("T Cells", "B Cells", "NK Cells"))
# save lymphocyte object
lymph_dir <- paste0(base_dir, "/annot_lvl1_lymphocyte.rds")
saveRDS(lymphocyte, lymph_dir)
```
